transcript: Jennifer Nettles writes beautiful music, but I'm not really sure that she was ready to write an entire musical by herself, as she wrote the book, Music, Lyrics and is starring in Giulia: the Poison Queen of Palermo, which just opened off Broadway. And while I think this show has a ton of potential, it never quite lives up to it. And I think the biggest thing holding it back is the depiction of Giulia herself, as the show refuses to depict her as anything other than the hero, despite the fact that she is a serial killer and poisons many, many people over the course of the show. She could be such a complex anti hero in the vein of Sweeney Todd, but instead the show takes great pains to make sure that every single murder is completely justified. She never gets carried away. No innocent people ever get caught in the crossfire. There are actually a few moments in the show where it seems like it is going to pivot into a more morally grey area, but every single time, without fail, it pivots into another far less interesting but more palatable direction. And as a result, she never really has to grapple with the weight of her actions. And honestly, all of the characters feel pretty shallow And one note. they are all either good or bad, with no in between. That way when the bad guys die, you don't feel conflicted at all. But in the Process, removing a lot of the complexity and intrigue that I think should be present in a story like this. And so I wish she had been able to partner with a book writer who could help her find the story. Writing a musical is hard, especially when you've never written one before. And so having someone with more experience on the writing team, I think, would have made a world of difference. because, like I said, the show has a ton of potential. A show about a female serial killer fighting back against the patriarchy could be really interesting. And the music is actually pretty good. It's very much not the style that I expected from her, given her country roots. It kind of straddles pop contemporary musical theatre and this lyrical, almost Hamilton esque patter. She definitely struggles a bit lyrically, and I do think that the pop contemporary musical theatre side of the score is stronger than the parts where it feels like it's trying to emulate Hamilton. But overall, she definitely proves that she is more than capable of writing a musical theatre score. And the cast all sound really great singing it. And with the help of an established book writer, I think the show could have been something really special. But as is, it just feels like a big missed opportunity.
